title: Cloud Computing: Concepts, Models, and Applications
topics: AI and Big Data in Cloud

bullets.text: Introduction to cloud computing and its importance in modern technology.
Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services over the internet.
Services include servers, storage, databases, networking, software, and AI.
It's a model of renting computing resources instead of owning and maintaining them.
Analogy: paying for electricity without owning the power plant.
On-demand self-service: users access resources as needed without human interaction.
Broad network access: services available over the internet from various devices.
Resource pooling: providers share resources across multiple customers securely.
Rapid elasticity: resources can scale up or down quickly based on demand.
Measured service: usage is monitored and billed according to resources consumed.
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): delivers fundamental computing resources like VMs, storage, networking (e.g., AWS EC2).
Platform as a Service (PaaS): provides infrastructure plus a development platform with built-in tools (e.g., Google App Engine).
Software as a Service (SaaS): delivers ready-to-use applications over the internet (e.g., Gmail, Microsoft 365, Zoom).
Public cloud: services delivered over the internet, shared by multiple organizations, cost-effective.
Private cloud: dedicated to a single organization, offers more control and security.
Hybrid cloud: combines public and private clouds for flexibility and security.
Community cloud: shared by several organizations with common goals or requirements.
Reduced costs: eliminates heavy investment in hardware, maintenance, and data centers.
Improved scalability: easily expand or reduce resources during peak or low times.
Enhanced flexibility: employees can access applications and data from anywhere.
Reliability: leading providers offer backup, disaster recovery, and high availability.
Supports innovation: faster experimentation and deployment of solutions.
Security and privacy: trusting providers to protect sensitive data on remote servers.
Downtime: outages can affect access to critical resources due to internet dependency.
Compliance: adherence to strict industry regulations for data storage.
Vendor lock-in: difficulty and cost associated with switching cloud providers.
Performance concerns: potential issues for applications requiring high speed or low latency.
Data storage and backup (e.g., Google Drive, Dropbox).
Business collaboration (e.g., Slack, Microsoft Teams) and entertainment streaming (e.g., Netflix, Spotify).
Healthcare (EHR, telemedicine) and education (online courses, virtual classrooms).
AI and Big Data Analytics: renting high-performance computing for data processing and machine learning.
Edge computing: processing data closer to the source (e.g., IoT devices) to reduce latency, still relies on cloud for storage.
Multi-cloud strategies: using services from multiple providers to avoid lock-in and improve reliability.
Serverless computing: developers focus on code, cloud provider manages infrastructure automatically.
Enhanced security and compliance: continued investment in encryption and advanced technologies.
Integration with AI, blockchain, and 5G to expand possibilities.
Summary of cloud computing's flexibility, scalability, cost savings, models, benefits, and challenges.
